title: Nord Stream Sabotage Trial Begins With Explosive Allegations Against Ukraine
desc:
Nord Stream Sabotage Trial Begins With Explosive Allegations Against Ukraine

Authored by RFE/RL staff via OilPrice.com,

  • A German court is trying former Ukrainian officer Serhii Kuznetsov over his alleged role in coordinating the September 2022 Nord Stream pipeline sabotage.

  • German prosecutors allege the operation was conducted on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities, although Kyiv denies involvement and no Ukrainian political leadership role has been established.

  • The trial could intensify political disputes in Germany over continued military assistance to Ukraine, particularly among opposition parties critical of Berlin's support.

After four years of speculation, leaks, and briefings by anonymous sources, the world is finally about to hear evidence given publicly under oath in a German courtroom about how the Nord Stream gas pipelines were blown up - in a case that could prove politically explosive.

German prosecutors have identified seven Ukrainian suspects, but just one of them is in the dock in the trial beginning on October 14. He is named as Serhii K. in court documents that say he is suspected of being an accomplice to a war crime.

That classification has caused outrage. But German prosecutors have further raised the stakes by stating the suspects were operating "on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine."

Kyiv has always strictly denied any involvement in the attack, which damaged crucial energy infrastructure serving Germany - one of its most important military backers in its fight since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Serhii K., who has been identified elsewhere as Serhiy Kuznetsov, says he is innocent.

'Two Crazy Military Men'

Nord Stream is majority-owned by Russia's state-controlled Gazprom and co-financed by major European energy companies. It was constructed to deliver Russian gas directly to Germany, bypassing transit states such as Ukraine and Poland, which had tense relations with Moscow.

The suspected sabotage and subsequent gas leaks happened in September 2022, rendering the pipelines as inoperable.

Western governments originally accused Russia of carrying out the blasts, but German investigators started forming a case that said a group of Ukrainian divers hired a yacht and planted explosives on the seabed.

They say Kuznetsov, a former military officer, was the ringleader.

"At the end of February 2022, he and other military personnel, on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine, developed the plan," says a summary of the indictment released by prosecutors. "The aim was to permanently halt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from the natural gas trade to finance its war efforts."

The prosecutors have not stated publicly the full extent of the alleged conspiracy.

The full indictment contains some further details, according to three German media outlets that say they have seen it: public-service TV station ARD and two print-era heavyweights, Sueddeutsche Zeitung and Die Zeit.

They all reported that, while in custody in Italy, Kuznetsov had phoned his wife in Kyiv and investigators were secretly listening in as he said he'd been advised by a lawyer that it was time to admit this had been "an official military operation." His commander should state that they were not just "two crazy military men."

Kuznetsov's Italian lawyer, Nicola Canestrini, has played down the importance of this evidence, saying there was "no smoking gun" in the case.

"It is hard to believe that, after Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, a German court should hold a war crimes trial against a Ukrainian serviceman," he added in comments to RFE/RL.

The three German media outlets named Roman Chervinskiy as Serhii K.'s commander, and his name also appeared in multiple earlier media reports citing intelligence sources. Chervinskiy told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service in July that "the Germans actually have no evidence whatsoever that Serhii took part in this operation, if it even took place."

Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z., is currently in custody in Croatia, where he is fighting extradition. He was previously detained in Poland but was freed when a Polish judge ruled that if Ukraine were responsible for the Nord Stream attack, it was a "just" act.

A professional diver identified by his Polish lawyers as Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, he was working in Croatia as an adviser on a Hollywood movie about Nord Stream.

During the trial, the prosecution will have to lay out its evidence for a conspiracy and the full extent of it.

"That is the crucial question: How much came from the top of the Ukrainian political system or how much was prepared by some insiders in the intelligence service?" Stefan Meister, a specialist on Russia and Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations, told RFE/RL.

"The key political question is the role of Zelenskyy and the presidential administration. And there we still have no proof that they were really involved," he added.

Kuznetsov's German lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp, said prosecutors "have not provided any direct, conclusive evidence of our client's involvement" and that the German court will have to determine whether Nord Stream was actually a legitimate military target.

The Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg has scheduled two hearings every week until at least February, with no specified end date yet.

German Support For Ukraine

As the case unfolds, it will also feed into bitter disputes in Germany about ongoing support for Ukraine. The main opposition party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), is highly critical of this support and calls for close ties to Russia instead.

Evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Nord Stream attack "would strengthen the AfD's argumentation against this support for Ukraine," said Meister. "They have all these narratives about Ukrainian corruption, a failed state.... It would resonate also in parts of German society."

The AfD has recently won key regional elections and is piling the pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government over Ukraine, immigration, and economic concerns.

Merz's response has been to double down on his current policies, including on Ukraine. Most recently, he was in Kyiv on October 4 with a new aid package including joint production of interceptors to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.

Mikhaylo Honchar, head of the Kyiv-based Strategy XXI Global Studies Center, told RFE/RL this would likely continue regardless of what comes out at the trial.

"If you take into consideration real Russian policy, which is directed against the EU and NATO, and Russia's anti-German rhetoric, I think the government of Germany will avoid steps which would undermine the bilateral relationship [with Ukraine]", he said.

He added that the prosecution case was "absurd," citing German media reports that the attack may have been a Russian false-flag operation.

But in any case, Honchar said, a guilty verdict would be met with a clear response in Ukraine. "Many people will say: 'If our guys did it, they are heroes.'"

title: NRC Approves Security Plan For NANO's Laser Enrichment Partner As SWU Spot Hit Record HIgh
desc:
NRC Approves Security Plan For NANO's Laser Enrichment Partner As SWU Spot Hit Record HIgh

Last week the uranium showed up. This week Washington signed off on who gets to look at what happens to it.

On Thursday morning LIS Technologies (LIST), the private laser enrichment developer in which NANO Nuclear is a shareholder and strategic partner, announced that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has approved its Standard Practice Procedures Plan (SPPP) for the Test Demonstration Facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the same building that, as we reported a week ago in "The Gas Station Gets Its Gas," took delivery of its first shipment of uranium hexafluoride (UF6) on October 8.

Two milestones in seven days, for a company that is still pre-revenue and that most investors had never heard of a year ago, is a remarkable clip for an industry which is desperately in need of modernization with electricity costs soaring across the US, and which usually measures progress in decades.

What The NRC Actually Approved

An SPPP sounds like paperwork, and it mostly is. But it is the paperwork that matters for this particular technology. The plan lays out the security procedures and controls for the facility's "closed area," the restricted space where LIST keeps classified matter tied to its proprietary CRISLA-4G laser enrichment process. The NRC found the plan meets the requirements of 10 CFR Part 25 (access authorization), 10 CFR Part 95 (facility security clearance and safeguarding of classified information) and 32 CFR Part 117 (the Pentagon's industrial security rulebook), and concluded it gives "reasonable assurance" that LIST will adequately protect the classified material and sensitive information in its possession.

Translation: laser enrichment know-how is treated as a national security secret, and before a company can keep doing classified work in Oak Ridge, it has to prove to the NRC that it can keep that secret. The same dynamic is why every enrichment technology in the West lives behind locked doors and security clearances, and away from prying Iranian spies: a process that can cheaply enrich uranium to reactor grade can, in the wrong hands, keep going...

LIST submitted the plan on February 11, so the review took 246 days which by NRC standards that is practically express delivery.

Two caveats worth flagging. First, the SPPP only takes full effect once LIST passes a successful NRC operational readiness review. Second, the approval is a stepping stone toward the item that actually matters, a possessing facility security clearance for the Oak Ridge site, which CEO Jay Yu called "the next step." In other words, Thursday's news unlocks the next door; a few more still stand between LIST and commercial enrichment which is the end game.

Christo Liebenberg, LIST's president and co-founder, explained why the company is celebrating a security plan:

"After decades working in laser enrichment, I know how carefully the NRC reviews these plans, so this approval means a great deal... The path to a facility security clearance runs through exactly this kind of demonstrated discipline, and clearing that bar is a necessary step toward taking our CRISLA technology from demonstration to commercial nuclear fuel production, as part of Project F.U.E.L. (Future Uranium Enrichment with Lasers)."

Director of Regulatory Affairs Julie Olivier was more succinct: the approval brings LIST "one step closer to licensing a full-capacity laser-based uranium enrichment facility."

One Week, Two Boxes Ticked

Regular readers have been following LIST since January, when the company unveiled a $1.4 billion laser enrichment project on the 206-acre "LIST Island" at the footprint of the Manhattan Project's K-25 gaseous diffusion plant. Since then it has bought a $6.2 million building next door for its isotope and deconversion pilots, started technical feasibility and environmental characterization work on LIST Island (August 20), received its first UF6 (October 8) and now cleared the NRC's security review.

Here is how the timeline looks, along with what is still left to do:

The sequencing matters. Last week's UF6 delivery lets LIST start optimizing its laser process on real feedstock, with the goal of reaching Technology Readiness Level 5 "in the coming months." Thursday's approval protects the classified side of that work. Neither puts a commercial plant in the ground - that will take some time - and LIST's own fine print says it can only make realistic economic predictions for a commercial facility after a successful Phase 2 pilot plant. But, and this is what matters to stock bulls, each step removes a reason to doubt the next one.

Why Anyone Should Care: SWU At A Record

None of this would rate a second post in a week if enrichment were plentiful. It is the opposite. As Jefferies' uranium team noted in its latest Uranium Market Update (available to pro subs), spot enrichment, which is measured in Separative Work Units, hit a series high of $215/SWU in August, against $181/SWU in the long-term market, and the prompt premium in enrichment is now wider than in conversion. Put differently, buyers are paying up for enrichment capacity they can get soon, because there is very little of it.

Spot SWU has more than quintupled from its 2018 trough, and it is now well above the 2009 peak.

Enrichment has also become a much bigger slice of what a utility pays for fuel. Jefferies estimates the spot-basis cost of enriched uranium product (EUP) at $4,366/kgU in August, up 15% YoY, with enrichment accounting for $1,340/kgU, or 31% of the total, and calls enrichment "a substantial source of incremental cost pressure."

And the West is short capacity at precisely the wrong moment: the US has a single commercial enrichment plant (Urenco's in Eunice, NM), the Russian import ban waivers run out in January 2028, and the DOE has been demanding a faster enrichment buildout while handing out $900 million checks each to Centrus, General Matter and Orano. Building centrifuge capacity is not getting any easier either: BofA just cut its price objective on Centrus (LEU) by 10%, the only uranium name in its coverage to get a cut, citing the "rising complexity of its substantial U.S. enrichment capacity build-out" (full note available to pro subs).

That is exactly the opening laser enrichment is supposed to fill: a smaller, modular, less energy-hungry way to make SWU. LIST is no longer alone in pitching it to Wall Street, either. Goldman's clean energy analyst Brian Lee, who hosted LIST's would-be competitor Quantum Leap Energy (the ASP Isotopes unit slated for a spin-off) on October 8, wrote in his note (available to pro subs) that the company is "focused on commercializing laser-based enrichment capabilities as well as uranium conversion," with the discussion centered on "the broader opportunity to address growing bottlenecks across the Western nuclear fuel cycle." When Goldman starts hosting laser enrichment roadshows, the theme has left the lab and the only question is which institutions will be the first to buy.

The NANO Angle

For NANO shareholders, the logic is the same as last week, just one step further along. Under their November 2024 collaboration agreement, LIST is NANO's preferred supplier of enriched UF6, and the two intend for LIST to supply that enriched UF6 to NANO at no cost, with LIST compensated via a profit-sharing arrangement that has yet to be finalized. NANO's job is to handle what comes after enrichment, which is why it bought an NRC-licensed deconversion site in Lea County, NM two weeks ago. Jay Yu, who runs LIST, is also NANO's founder, so the related-party questions we raised last week haven't gone anywhere.

We summarized the setup in a tweet when last week's milestone hit:

The Gas Station Gets Its Gas: NANO's Laser Enrichment Partner Takes Delivery Of Its First Uranium https://t.co/2TNrWemf5H

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 8, 2026

The market, for its part, remains unimpressed: NNE was down about 3% at $12.58 Thursday morning with short interest back to record high just shy of 40% of float. Then again, a security plan approval is the kind of milestone that never moves a stock on the day, and always shows up in hindsight.

And for those keeping score of the alternatives, Vivek Ramaswamy's nuclear startup is betting on a reactor design that skips enrichment altogether, which tells you how big the bottleneck has become: some developers would rather redesign the reactor than wait in the SWU line (good luck to them).

Bottom Line

In a week, LIST went from an empty test loop to a test loop with uranium in it and an NRC-approved plan to protect the classified process that will run on it. The hard parts are still ahead: the readiness review, the facility security clearance, TRL 5, a Phase 2 pilot and roughly $1.4 billion of financing for a commercial plant. Lasers have also broken plenty of hearts before (ask anyone who worked on AVLIS).

But with spot SWU at a record, the Russian import waivers expiring in just over a year and even the incumbent centrifuge builders running into complexity, the West needs every credible enrichment path it can get. As Jay Yu put it Thursday, the goal is to make LIST "the nation's leader in nuclear laser enrichment innovation." We have argued for years that whoever controls the fuel will collect the rent long after the reactor startups finish raising money; this week, the fuel side of NANO's stack got two steps closer to collecting it.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf said in a televised speech on Wednesday that the US must be "punished" in order for it to accept Iran's demands to end the war.

Ghalibaf made the comments in the context of the latest response Iran received from the US in indirect negotiations, which Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has called "inadequate" because Washington didn’t agree to all of Tehran's conditions.

"The United States must be punished, change its behavior, and be made to understand unequivocally that it must accept the legitimate demands of the Iranian nation," Ghalibaf said, according to Iran’s PressTV.

Iran is essentially asking the US to fulfill its obligations under the Memorandum of Understanding that the two nations signed back in June, which would require the US to end its blockade of Iran, provide some sanctions relief, release frozen Iranian funds, and ensure an end to Israel’s war in Lebanon.

Ghalibaf, who was deeply involved in the MoU negotiations, said he ensured the MoU included two parts because he didn’t trust the US.

The parliament speaker also said that Iran must be prepared for both negotiations and fighting with the aim of establishing deterrence to prevent future attacks. "On the battlefield, before God, we must believe that we should fight courageously against our coercive enemy, while also engaging in negotiations to establish lasting deterrence," he said.

He invoked the Iran-Iraq War, which lasted from 1980 to 1988, suggesting Tehran is preparing for the possibility of a very prolonged conflict with the US. During the Iran-Iraq War, the US backed Saddam Hussein by providing intelligence and other types of support while being aware that he was using chemical weapons against Iran.

Ghalibaf fought for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) throughout the war and rose through the ranks to become a senior combat commander. In his remarks on Wednesday, Ghalibaf pointed to the conflict as an example of Iran establishing deterrence.

"In the eight years of sacred defense, we fought against Saddam’s Baathist regime. Of course, we paid a price, we suffered hardships, but in the end, for several decades, no one dared or had the desire to attack our beloved country, Iran," he said.

title: MS NOW Retracts Report That FBI Director Kash Patel Landed In Russia
desc:
MS NOW Retracts Report That FBI Director Kash Patel Landed In Russia

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

MS NOW has retracted a report that FBI Director Kash Patel landed in Russia on Oct. 14.

"We regret this error," Ken Dilanian, an MS Now reporter, said on air during an afternoon show.

MS Now host Peter Alexander had said during a broadcast on Wednesday morning that he had breaking news to report - that Patel "has landed in Russia for a meeting scheduled to take place there." He attributed the reporting to two anonymous sources, or two people "familiar with the matter."

The FBI responded by posting a video of Patel at an event at Liberty University in Virginia. Members of Congress, including Rep. John McGuire (R-Va.), also shared photographs of themselves with Patel at the event.

"MS Now's 'sources' are 'familiar' with NOTHING!" the FBI said in a post on X.

Ben Williamson, an FBI spokesman, wrote in another post on the social media platform: "I have had many strange experiences in life, but in tier 1 had to be seeing a clip of MS Now reporting breaking news that Kash Patel has 'just landed in Russia' - right as I'm receiving pics of Kash Patel doing a law enforcement appreciation event today in Lynchburg, Virginia."

Dilanian said during a show hosted by Alicia Menendez later Wednesday that the network had "since learned that Patel did not, in fact, land in Russia today and remains in the U.S."

After saying the FBI had not answered MS Now's questions about the purported trip, Dilanian referenced reports alleging Patel has a planned meeting in Russia and added that some Democrats have told Patel not to attend.

"But we do know now that he has not already landed in Russia, as we reported earlier. The timing of any potential trip remains unclear," Dilanian said. "Again, we regret this error, and we are transparent about when we make errors."

The Society of Professional Journalists recommends that outlets identify sources whenever feasible and, if using unnamed sources, include as much information as possible without revealing details that could lead to them being identified.

MS Now did not respond to questions, including whether it plans to work with the same sources moving forward, by the time of publication.

MS Now removed a video that featured a former FBI agent commenting on the report. The former agent had called Patel a "babe in the woods" when it came to Russia. It also posted Dilanian's apology on its website.

"This reporting has been updated in keeping with our policy of transparency, including promptly correcting any errors," the outlet said.

President Donald Trump recently banned MS Now and several other outlets from the White House, saying they consistently reported fake news. A federal judge blocked the ban as the outlets' legal case against it proceeds. The government has appealed the block.

Patel, following the correction, wrote in an Oct. 14 post on X, "From Russia, with Love..."

He also said MS Now "constantly tells lies about this FBI and law enforcement's historic achievements in safeguarding the American people."

"The US suggested several possible methods for unfreezing the assets, including for them to be moved into a new special-purpose financial vehicle overseen by Washington," the sources said.

"Those are assets that are frozen ​in Europe and they should remain frozen in Europe. ​This is our business and we are deciding over ⁠it," Merz said in Brussels ahead of an EU ​summit.

"Britain is getting the dregs," GB News presenter Patrick Christys urged, reacting to the case of an Iraqi man who crossed the Channel, gave a false name, and lived undetected for weeks before German authorities tipped off the UK National Crime Agency.

He arrived by small boat from France in August 2025, claimed asylum, and was placed in a Home Office hotel in Oldham, Greater Manchester. NCA officers arrested him there in October 2025, but only after Germany flagged his background.

He is now fighting extradition to face terrorism-related charges and an allegation of raping a German woman. The allegations have not been established in court.

His lawyer, Joanna Curtis, told a Westminster hearing that extradition would be inhumane because "he has significant mental health issues, including severe anxiety, as well as depression." She linked the trauma to a bomb attack in Iraq that killed his son and even laughably cited symptoms of "pins and needles."

This is not an isolated failure. Earlier this year, another ISIS-linked man reached Britain the same way after social media reassured him the UK takes everyone.

Mohammed Yaseen, previously convicted in Germany for ISIS membership, attended beheadings and floggings in Iraq, then crossed after watching TikTok videos claiming Britain "accepts everyone and respects human rights."

He gave false details, was processed, and only later identified by biometrics. Prosecutors described him as high risk.

The pattern is clear: people with documented extremist histories clear the Channel, destroy or withhold documents, and enter the asylum system before any meaningful check occurs.

The scale makes individual cases inevitable. Small-boat arrivals since Labour took office have already surpassed the strength of the British Army.

More than 83,000 crossed between July 2024 and September 2026, exceeding the Army's roughly 83,000 regulars and outnumbering the Navy and RAF combined.

Total arrivals since 2018 top 200,000. The vast majority are military-aged men. Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp called it "completely bonkers," noting Labour had "let an entire army-sized population cross the Channel illegally."

Reform leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly warned the crossings represent a national security emergency.

At this week's Prime Minister's Questions he pressed Andy Burnham directly: "Every week there are young, unidentified males from Iran coming into this country, some of whom pose a genuine security threat to our nation. Is it not time the Government recognises that what is going on in the English Channel is a national security emergency?"

Burnham replied that crossings were "coming down" and removals were up, while acknowledging more needed to be done. Farage has described the situation as an "out-of-control disaster."

The numbers are not sustainable on any measure. Settlement grants alone have reached one every minute.

title: States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Gives Young Users Dangerous Advice
desc:
States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Gives Young Users Dangerous Advice

Authored by Jill McLaughlin via The Epoch Times,

Eight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI Oct. 14, claiming the company's ChatGPT app harms children, deceives parents, and violates state consumer fraud laws.

The states - Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, and Arizona - individually filed lawsuits in their states, alleging the chatbot was giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide while pretending to be a friend.

"We will not just accept that any big tech company can make money by hurting Iowa's kids and use them as lab rats in a race to be the first, or the biggest, or have the most users," Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird told reporters Wednesday during a news conference on the lawsuits.

Chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) are becoming increasingly popular with teens. Almost two-thirds - 64 percent - of teens ages 13 to 17 reported using chatbots, with about 30 percent using them every day, according to a report published in December 2025 by Pew Research Center.

ChatGPT is by far the most popular among teens and favored by 59 percent of them, the survey found.

The lawsuits filed Wednesday claim ChatGPT is marketed by OpenAI as a safe product but, in reality, it is designed to be dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and coaches them to commit suicide or to harm other people.

The states are asking the courts to compel OpenAI to comply with state consumer fraud laws, which prohibit deceptive business practices.

OpenAI responded to the filing of lawsuits, saying the company has implemented several safety measures and is continuing to work to build more safeguards.

"We've built industry-leading, age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack," OpenAI's spokesman Eric Porterfield told The Epoch Times in an email. "While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today."

The company is committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, according to Porterfield.

OpenAI claims its chatbot is intended for users age 13 and older. Users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it.

ChatGPT for Teens applies default safeguards for users under 18, OpenAI claims. Teens can manage and delete their chats and history, and control whether their conversations are used by the company to train models.

The company claims 90 percent of its teen ChatGPT users only use it for learning, skill-building, or productivity. Half of the teens who use it for conversations take breaks when they are given a break reminder, according to OpenAI.

Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said the states moved ahead with lawsuits instead of waiting for Congress to set federal guidelines.

"We're in a world right now where the AI companies - and in this case OpenAI - are asked to police themselves," said Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach during Wednesday's press conference. "And as our cases allege, they've done a very poor job of policing themselves and have placed the public in danger."

Florida became the first state to file a lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman in June, alleging its chatbot concealed serious risks, suppressed internal safety warnings, and deceived Floridians.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier launched a criminal investigation into OpenAI in April after ChatGPT gave detailed advice to a suspected shooter who allegedly used it in a deadly campus shooting at Florida State University last year.

title: Why Diesel Prices Are So Much Higher Than Gasoline
desc:
Why Diesel Prices Are So Much Higher Than Gasoline

Authored by Robert Rapier via OilPrice.com,

  • Diesel has generally cost more than gasoline since 2004 due to higher production costs, taxes, and global demand.

  • Global refinery disruptions, export restrictions, and low inventories have widened the diesel price premium in 2026.

  • Strong US crude production and refinery output cannot fully offset global diesel supply shortages.

There was a time when diesel fuel was usually cheaper than gasoline in the United States. That relationship began to change about 20 years ago, and since then diesel has generally traded at a premium. Today, that premium is not just persistent but unusually large, which raises an obvious question: how did we get from gasoline typically costing more than diesel to diesel costing substantially more than gasoline?

The answer has two parts.

The first is structural and goes back to the mid-2000s, when changes in fuel specifications, taxes, refining economics, and global demand fundamentally altered the relationship between gasoline and diesel prices.

The second is more immediate. In 2026, refinery disruptions, geopolitical conflicts, low inventories, and reduced exports from major suppliers have pushed the global diesel market into an unusually tight position. Understanding the difference between those long-term and short-term forces explains both why diesel usually costs more and why the gap is so large right now.

Diesel Was Once The Cheaper Fuel

Before the mid-2000s, diesel was often cheaper than regular gasoline in the United States. There were exceptions, particularly during cold winters when heating-oil demand strengthened, but the longer-term pattern generally favored diesel. That began to change around 2004, and according to the Energy Information Administration, on-highway diesel prices have been higher than regular gasoline prices almost continuously since September of that year.

That shift is clearly visible in the historical data I examined in my 2023 article on the subject. In the decade before 2005, gasoline generally traded at a small premium to diesel. After that, the relationship reversed, and diesel became the more expensive fuel in most years. The timing is important because it coincided with a major change in the way U.S. refiners had to produce highway diesel.

Ultra-Low-Sulfur Diesel Changed The Economics

Beginning in the mid-2000s, U.S. refiners had to dramatically reduce the sulfur content of highway diesel. That was an important environmental improvement because sulfur emissions contribute to air pollution and acid rain, but it also made diesel more expensive to produce. Refineries invested billions of dollars in new hydrotreating and sulfur-removal equipment, and those investments increased capital and operating costs and made compliant diesel more expensive to produce and distribute.

My earlier article focused heavily on this transition because the timing lines up closely with the point at which diesel's historical discount disappeared. EIA now describes the persistent diesel premium as the result of several factors working together, including strong global demand for diesel and other distillates, the higher cost of producing low-sulfur diesel, and federal taxes that are six cents per gallon higher on diesel than on gasoline.

None of those factors explains every short-term price movement, but together they created a structural premium that had not existed to the same degree before 2004. Once diesel became more expensive to produce and more tightly linked to global distillate markets, the old relationship with gasoline never really returned.

Diesel Became A Global Commodity

Another important change has been the globalization of the diesel market. Gasoline is also traded internationally, but diesel and other middle distillates occupy an especially important role in the global economy because they power trucking, agriculture, construction, mining, shipping, industrial equipment, and heating systems. Strong demand in Europe, China, India, and the United States has kept pressure on global distillate balances for years.

That means U.S. diesel prices are increasingly influenced by events far beyond U.S. borders. Even when domestic production is strong, refiners can export diesel into higher-priced international markets, tying domestic prices more closely to global supply and demand. This is one reason it is misleading to look only at U.S. crude oil production and assume that abundant domestic oil should automatically translate into cheap diesel.

The United States can produce plenty of crude while still facing tight supplies of refined products. Crude oil has to be processed in the right refineries, into the right products, and then moved through the right transportation system. Those constraints matter just as much as the amount of oil coming out of the ground.

2022 Showed How Quickly The Premium Can Explode

The most dramatic recent example came in 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy markets. Diesel was hit particularly hard. Russia was a major supplier of crude oil, refined products, and feedstocks to Europe and other markets, so sanctions and trade restrictions forced a rapid reshuffling of global flows. Gasoline prices rose sharply as well, but diesel supplies tightened even more, pushing the diesel premium to record levels.

In my earlier article, I noted that the gasoline-diesel spread reached a record in 2022. At the time, the disruption from Russia explained why a structural premium suddenly became an extreme one. The market eventually adjusted as trade routes shifted, refinery operations stabilized, and inventories recovered, but that normalization did not last.

Why The Gap Is So Large Again In 2026

The current situation resembles 2022 in one important respect: global diesel supply has again been disrupted more severely than gasoline supply. EIA recently reported that global distillate supplies are tight because of reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East. At the same time, U.S. refiners have been running near maximum utilization, with domestic distillate production averaging about 5.1 million barrels per day through August, the highest level since 2019.

That point is worth emphasizing because it shows that the current problem is not simply a collapse in U.S. refinery output. American refiners are producing large volumes of diesel, but global demand for those barrels has increased at the same time that supplies elsewhere have fallen. As exports increased, U.S. inventories declined, and by mid-September distillate inventories were about 13% below the five-year seasonal average even though summer is normally a period when inventories build ahead of winter.

Since then, the global situation has become even tighter. Russia has restricted diesel exports as refinery infrastructure has been damaged, China has curtailed fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, and Middle Eastern refining and shipping have been disrupted by the conflict involving Iran. Tanker costs and insurance rates have also risen, making it more expensive to move refined products around the world.

The result is a global scramble for middle distillates. Both gasoline and diesel are affected by higher crude prices, but diesel is being squeezed more severely because the product itself is in shorter supply relative to demand. That is why the diesel-gasoline spread has widened so dramatically.

The Price Gap Is Now Extraordinary

As of October 5, the national average price of on-highway diesel was $6.199 per gallon, compared with $4.354 for regular gasoline - a spread of about $1.85 per gallon. Diesel reached a nominal record of $6.29 per gallon in September, according to EIA, and remained above $6 nationally in early October.

That gap is not primarily the result of a sudden increase in diesel taxes or some new change in fuel specifications. Those structural factors help explain why diesel usually costs more than gasoline, but they do not explain why the premium is so large today. The current premium reflects a very tight global distillate market layered on top of the long-term changes that already made diesel the more expensive fuel.

That distinction is important because it separates the underlying reason diesel normally carries a premium from the temporary forces that can cause that premium to explode.

Refining Margins Are A Consequence, Not A Cause

Refining margins have risen sharply, and major refiners are benefiting from the tight market. But those high margins are a consequence of constrained diesel supply relative to demand rather than the original cause of the shortage.

When refinery capacity is disrupted, exports are curtailed, and inventories fall, the value of the remaining barrels rises. Refiners that can continue producing diesel benefit from that scarcity, but the scarcity comes first. This distinction is important because high margins are sometimes cited as evidence that refiners decided to raise prices, when in reality the margin expansion is largely the market's response to a shortage of refined product.

Diesel Is A Different Market Than Gasoline

The broader lesson is that gasoline and diesel may come from the same barrel of crude oil, but they are not interchangeable products. They serve different markets, have different seasonal demand patterns, require different processing, and face different global supply pressures. A refinery cannot simply turn every barrel of crude into whichever product happens to be most expensive that day because refinery configuration, crude quality, product specifications, and physical operating limits all constrain what can be produced.

That is why abundant crude oil does not guarantee cheap diesel. The United States can produce record amounts of oil, run refineries near capacity, and still face expensive diesel if global product markets remain tight.

Twenty years ago, gasoline was often the more expensive fuel. Then diesel moved to a structural premium, and today that premium has widened dramatically because the global market for diesel and other middle distillates is again under severe strain. Until those supply constraints ease, diesel is likely to remain much more expensive than gasoline.

title: "De-Risk As Fast As Possible": EU Eyes Vietnam For Critical Materials To Cut Alarming China Dependence
desc:
"De-Risk As Fast As Possible": EU Eyes Vietnam For Critical Materials To Cut Alarming China Dependence

Brussels appears increasingly aligned with the Trump administration's view that securing reliable, conflict-free supplies of critical materials is important for the incoming rearmament supercycle. Continued reliance on China exposes Western defense manufacturers to export restrictions that have already disrupted supply chains and could delay deliveries.

Reuters cites internal EU documents dated June 2026 that identified Vietnam as a potential source of critical materials outside China.

"Considering Europe's need to rearm and de-risk as fast as possible, the EU cannot afford ignoring Vietnam as a potential supplier of critical raw materials considering its abundant reserves in rare earth and tungsten in particular," the document stated which was prepared by the EU delegation in Hanoi.

The push comes as Chinese export restrictions collide with the West's rearmament supercycle next year, exposing alarming vulnerabilities in the supply chains needed to manufacture missiles, ammunition, armored vehicles, one-way attack drones, interceptors, sensors, and other military equipment.

The West is quickly learning that bigger and bigger defense budgets alone cannot solve the critical material shortage and there is high urgency in securing alternative supply chains.

Vietnam holds substantial deposits of tungsten, rare earths, and other critical minerals, but its exports to Europe have largely been limited to tungsten and antimony, both of which are used to manufacture weapons.

The document noted that China's restrictions on critical material exports last year disrupted European supply chains, strengthening the case for exploring alternative sources.

It called for stronger relations with Vietnam to "add an alternative to China," especially after Beijing's export restrictions last year "disrupted European supply chains."

"The European Commission is currently assessing the potential for concrete cooperation with Vietnam in the critical raw materials sector," a spokesperson for the EU executive arm told the outlet.

Adrien Rabier, Bernstein's equity analyst covering European aerospace and defense, outlined to clients last month that Europe's rearmament supercycle will begin next year and extend through the end of the decade.

Our reporting has pointed out that the next phase of the critical materials trade will favor miners already producing and delivering these materials to Western markets.

This comes as resource nationalism intensifies across critical minerals, metals, energy, adding to uncertainty as the world heads into a potentially volatile winter.

The VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX), which tracks global companies that produce, refine, and recycle critical minerals, peaked in May and lost nearly half its value by early fall.

REMX's decline appears to be a retracement of the rally in 2025 and early 2026 that followed China's export restrictions. Once the space bottoms, traders will likely focus on miners that can reliably deliver conflict-free materials to the West. These materials are critical not only to the rearmament cycle but also to AI data centers, reindustrialization, electrification, and the broader modern economy.

title: 'Newspeak': Oxford University Tells Staff To Avoid Everyday English Phrases
desc:
'Newspeak': Oxford University Tells Staff To Avoid Everyday English Phrases

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

Oxford University has advised its staff to avoid common English idioms such as "learn the ropes" and "find your feet," on the grounds that they may confuse international students or that they perpetuate negative stereotypes.

The guidance appears in the university's official style guide, which also recommends replacing gendered terms and softer language around socioeconomic status, prompting criticism from free speech groups that Oxford is prioritising sensitivity over cultural immersion.

The style guide tells writers to favour "plain English" and cautions: "Be mindful of idioms that may not be familiar to international readers or that may use stereotypes. Use common words, short sentences and familiar constructions."

Oxford University guide ditches traditional British phrases in favour of 'inclusive' language for foreign students https://t.co/K3S44IcKQe

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 12, 2026

Specific alternatives are offered: "learn the ropes" becomes "learn how to do that," "find your feet" becomes "getting used to their new environment," and "blindspots" becomes "gaps in knowledge."

Gendered words face similar treatment. "Spokesman," "chairwoman," and "mankind" are to be swapped for "spokesperson," "chair," and "humankind."

Staff are also advised to use "they/them" rather than alternating "he" and "she," to describe "deprived" students as "lower income" or as having experienced "socioeconomic disadvantage," and to prefer "gay" over "homosexual" (except in legal or medical contexts) and "older people" over "the elderly."

Around a third of Oxford's students are international, including a fifth of undergraduates. The university has become increasingly dependent on higher fees from overseas students as domestic funding pressures grow.

An Oxford spokesman said: "Like many large organisations, including newspapers, Oxford University has a style guide to help staff write clearly and consistently. As a global university with staff and students from around the world, we write for a wide international audience. The guide provides practical advice for written University communications, from punctuation to choosing language that readers will readily understand. Its writing guidance is advisory and supports staff in exercising their own judgement about the language they use and the audience they are writing for."

Lord Young of the Free Speech Union rejected the premise. "Surely, one of the reasons international students come to Oxford is so that they can immerse themselves in our culture and master colloquial English," he said. "What's next? Is Oxford going to insist all lectures have to be in Esperanto?"

The episode fits a wider pattern of language policing across British higher education and politics. Cambridge University has previously argued that free speech should be restricted in certain circumstances.

Other institutions have declared the term "ethnic minority" itself offensive.

UK students have been ordered to undertake white privilege training.

The government has urged schools to report "anti-Muslim hostility."

The Green Party has called for the words "mother" and "father" to be erased in favour of more inclusive alternatives.

These measures arrive as universities face financial strain and recruit more heavily from overseas. Critics argue the result is a slow dilution of the very cultural and linguistic distinctiveness that draws international students in the first place.

Learning everyday English, including its idioms, is part of mastering the language rather than an obstacle to be removed. Treating common British phrases as potentially confusing or stereotypical places the burden of adaptation on the host culture instead of on those who choose to study within it.

The style guide is presented as advisory. In practice, such documents shape institutional expectations and signal which forms of expression are considered acceptable. Free speech advocates note that once everyday language is flagged as risky, the scope of self-censorship expands.

Oxford's response emphasises clarity for a global audience. Lord Young's reply highlights the opposite priority: that international students benefit from encountering the language and culture as it is used.

British universities remain among the world's leading institutions. Their reputation rests on rigorous standards and open inquiry, not on rewriting ordinary English and instituting Orwellian Newspeak to minimise every possible misunderstanding.

Treating common idioms as problems to be solved by avoidance rather than explanation reverses the traditional purpose of a world-class university. Students who arrive at Oxford should leave more fluent in the language and more familiar with the culture, not less exposed to either.

title: Iran Hormuz Attack Spree Starts Choking Oil Flows (Again), UBS Warns
desc:
Iran Hormuz Attack Spree Starts Choking Oil Flows (Again), UBS Warns

A surge in Iranian drone attacks on commercial ships appears to be weighing on Middle Eastern energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz, with 24 attacks reported so far this month. The latest reports indicate that two Emirati container ships were struck and sank in the narrow waterway within the past 24 hours.

UBS energy expert Henri Patricot told clients on Wednseday morning that crude and petroleum-product flows exiting the Gulf of Oman dropped to 9.1 million barrels a day over the past couple of days. The weekly average slipped to 13.5 million, compared with an early-October peak of 17 million.

Patricot provided more color on deteriorating shipping conditions in the Strait of Hormuz:

More attacks around Hormuz and in Saudi Arabia

Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and in the Gulf of Oman continue to be reported at the highest intensity since the start of the conflict (Figure 24).

Iran is reportedly using a new strategy to target ships, including using spotters in small boats. The attacks appear to be having a clearer negative impact on traffic via Hormuz in recent days. Separately, attacks have also continued in Saudi Arabia, with reports that Aramco's HQ which was targeted overnight.

Oil flows falling further; LNG holding up at much lower level

The latest data point to a more material drop in exports from the Middle East. UBS Evidence Lab data (> Access Dataset) indicate that crude and product flows out of the Gulf of Oman dropped to 9.1Mb/d in the past couple of days and have averaged 13.5Mb/d in the past week vs. a peak of 17Mb/d in early October (Figure 3).

Our estimate of combined crude and product exports through Hormuz and bypass routes is down to 9.5Mb/d over the past week, well below the recent high of 16Mb/d and September average of 14Mb/d (Figure 2).

Flows are still likely to be revised higher but there now appears to be a clear trend of declining flows since early October now. We are adding a new chart showing LNG flows out of the Gulf of Oman (Figure 4).

There has been an improvement in flows since mid-September and they are holding up for now, but only at ~25% of pre-conflict levels, vs. oil close close to 50% in the past week and 75% at recent peak.

Crude loadings rebound

On the positive side, Gulf crude loadings excluding Iran bounced back to >12Mb/d over the past couple of days. As loadings in previous days were revised higher too, October loadings are back up to 8.7Mb/d on average, in line the September average (Figure 12).

There is still no Iranian crude loading (Figure 13).

Outside Hormuz, preliminary data show no loadings from Yanbu in the past couple of days, taking the average to 1.6Mb/d so far in October, below the September average of 2.7Mb/d (Figure 16). Including Fujairah, bypass crude loadings averaged 2.1Mb/d over the past couple of days and 3.3Mb/d in October, vs. 5.4Mb/d in September. Gulf product loadings have ticked up just above 1Mb/d, still well below normal levels of >3Mb/d (Figure 17).

title: NATO's De Facto Expansion To The Caspian Sea Is Inevitable
desc:
NATO's De Facto Expansion To The Caspian Sea Is Inevitable

Authored by Andrew Korybko via Substack,

Russia still has time to propose Ukrainian-like security guarantees for averting another special operation...

Politico recently published a piece about how "France and Turkey block NATO's drive to deepen ties with Caucasus countries", not because they're opposed to it in principle, but due to Turkiye blocking the renewal of Armenia's partnership plan after France declined to approve Azerbaijan's. France and Azerbaijan have long been at odds over Paris' support of Armenia, particularly in the context of the Karabakh Conflict, and recently over Azerbaijan's detention of French citizens (who were later released).

Per Politico, "The delay has forced NATO to temporarily extend Armenia and Azerbaijan's outdated partnerships despite negotiations on the new plans being near-finalized, three of the diplomats said. The new plans would allow their participation in joint military exercises, boost military-to-military training and intensify cultural cooperation all the way down to setting up local English-language lessons, they added." Joint NATO drills might be held on the Caspian coast with Azerbaijan upon its plan's approval.

None of this is surprising to astute observers. August 2025's "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity" (TRIPP) has the unstated dual purpose of a NATO military logistics corridor to the Caspian Sea and thenceforth to Central Asia. TRIPP is therefore the means through which NATO aims to contain Russia along the southern flank of the new "cordon sanitaire" that Trump 2.0 assembled around it. Azerbaijan poses a Ukrainian-like challenge to Russia by functioning as TRIPP's irreplaceable transit state.

If Azerbaijan cooperated with Russia to ensure that TRIPP wouldn't be exploited for military purposes, then there wouldn't be any problem, but Baku has no such interests and has instead thrown its weight behind the West. In point of fact, President Ilham Aliyev announced last November that his country's armed forces have completed the conformation to NATO standards, and their naval drones could threaten Russia's Caspian Fleet in crisis scenarios just like Ukraine's currently threaten its Black Sea one.

Azerbaijan is also on pace to further integrate its economy with the EU's. Not only is it helping the bloc replace Russian energy, but it's also going to facilitate their trade with Central Asia, to which end European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced last month that "we will aim to crowd in up to €12 billion in public and private investment" in regional logistics along what's known as the "Middle Corridor". All of this tightens the containment noose around Russia's southern flank.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov suggested last month that his people are sometimes optimistic to the point of implied naivete and also tend not to proactively address latent crises. With the deepest of respect for those of them who are responsible for formulating its policies, that arguably appears to be the case regarding the threat that TRIPP poses to Russia. That's not to imply that Russia should wage a preventive war against Azerbaijan, just that it should urgently wise up to the threats coming from it.

Looking forward, just like NATO's de facto expansion to the Caspian Sea is inevitable, so too is it inevitable that Russia's threat perception towards Azerbaijan will intensify. The sooner, the better, since Russia still has time to propose Ukrainian-like security guarantees for averting another special operation. In this context, they could concern Azerbaijan agreeing to Russian inspections of TRIPP's cargo and not allowing any joint NATO drills on its territory, but Aliyev might not assent unless Putin presses him a bit.

title: Germany Puts Ukrainian Ex-Officer On Trial For Nord Stream "War Crime" As Defense Says Pipelines Were Fair Game
desc:
Germany Puts Ukrainian Ex-Officer On Trial For Nord Stream "War Crime" As Defense Says Pipelines Were Fair Game

Four years after the largest act of infrastructure sabotage in postwar Europe, Germany finally has a defendant. Just one.

Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian army officer, went on trial Wednesday at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg, accused of leading the seven-person team that blew up three of the four Nord Stream lines on September 26, 2022. Prosecutors charge him as a co-perpetrator of a war crime, namely an attack on civilian objects, along with causing an explosion, destroying structures and disrupting public utilities. Around 30 hearing days are scheduled, running into February.

The prosecution's version is about as cinematic as it gets: a crew of four professional divers, an explosives expert and a skipper set out from Rostock on the chartered yacht Andromeda, rented through intermediaries with forged identity papers, and planted devices packed with HMX and RDX at roughly 80 meters near the Danish island of Bornholm. Kuznietsov, a former SBU officer, allegedly ran the show from the deck. German investigators also say he incriminated himself by chatting about the operation with friends and relatives while in Italian custody, which in hindsight may not have been the best use of his phone privileges.

Most notable, however, is who Berlin says was behind it. The federal prosecutor's indictment states plainly that Kuznietsov and fellow servicemen were acting on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities, with the aim of permanently halting gas flows and cutting off Russia's revenue to fund the war. In other words, Germany is prosecuting an ally's officer for an operation it says the ally's state ordered, against German energy infrastructure, while continuing to bankroll that same ally. Kyiv, for its part, maintains it had nothing to do with it; Ukraine's prosecutor general said in July it had found "no evidence" of state involvement. Awkwardly, Ukraine's own human rights ombudsman had already confirmed to an Italian court that Kuznietsov was serving in the armed forces at the time.

On day one, the defense declined to let Kuznietsov speak and moved to dismiss all charges. His lawyers argued that war crimes prosecutions would be better aimed at Russian forces (citing Bucha and the deportation of Ukrainian children), that his fingerprints were never found on the yacht, and that no witness placed him aboard. His Ukrainian counsel go further, arguing the pipelines were a legitimate military target regardless of who hit them. The court has already rejected his claim to combatant immunity, ruling that it does not cover covert operations in which soldiers cannot be distinguished from civilians. The BBC reports the defense plans to submit written testimony from two of his former commanders, one of them reportedly the alleged mastermind of the entire operation, which should make for an interesting exhibit.

Then there is the matter of who wants a seat at the table. Gazprom-owned Nord Stream 2 AG has applied to join the case as a co-plaintiff, and Kuznietsov's Ukrainian lawyers warn that a conviction could hand Moscow a legal basis to claim compensation, potentially from the roughly $300 billion in frozen Russian assets that Europe has been trying to earmark for Kyiv. A guilty verdict, then, could put Brussels in the unusual position of having established a Russian damages claim against money it already promised to Ukraine.

The diver who keeps getting away

Kuznietsov is the only person currently on trial because Germany's second suspect keeps slipping through European courts. Volodymyr Zhuravliov, the alleged diver, was arrested in Poland in September 2025, only for a Warsaw court to refuse extradition a month later, ruling the act had been committed in the context of Russia's war. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was blunter, saying handing him over would go against Poland's interests and that those who built Nord Stream 2 "should be ashamed and remain silent."

Germany, whose energy costs have exploded - no pun intended - after the pipeline sabotage, and refuses to be ashamed or silent now that its entire manufacturing sector is imploding as a result, tried again in August when Croatian police picked up Zhuravliov in Pula, where he was reportedly working on, of all things, a Hollywood dramatization of the Nord Stream attack. Berlin upgraded its warrant to include the war crime charge, and on September 18 a Pula court approved extradition. His lawyers are appealing to Croatia's high criminal court and say they will go to international bodies if needed, so his arrival in Hamburg is anything but assured. According to ARD, investigators have identified seven suspects in total, one of whom has since been killed fighting Russia.

The question nobody in Hamburg will ask

The trial also formally enshrines the "six guys on a sailboat" thesis that first surfaced in March 2023 and was fleshed out by the WSJ in August 2024, when the Journal reported that Zelensky initially approved the plan before calling it off at the CIA's request, only for then-commander Valery Zaluzhny to proceed anyway. Zaluzhny, now ambassador in London, called it a provocation. The court is unlikely to spend much time on Seymour Hersh's February 2023 account, which pinned the operation on the US Navy, or on Joe Biden's February 2022 promise that if Russia invaded, "we will bring an end to it."

Meanwhile, the pipelines remain at the bottom of the Baltic, Nord Stream 1 having moved nearly 60 billion cubic meters in 2021, and Germany continues to pay up for LNG. The AfD has campaigned on restarting Russian gas flows, which means the verdict, due sometime next year, will land squarely in German domestic politics. Expect a long, carefully narrow trial in which a court determines whether one man captained a yacht, while the question of who sent the yacht remains politely unexamined.
